paras: The threatened lynching near Prosperity, South Carolina, took place in August 1888, when neighbors of Wade H. Suber in Newberry County accused an unnamed Black wagon driver of murdering and robbing him and seriously considered lynching him. The threat ended when Suber was found alive and well at Spartanburg.

Suber lived with Abraham Moore near Prosperity. On August 13 he took a bale of cotton belonging to Moore into town, sold it, and set out, apparently for home, in the wagon that had carried the cotton.

Suber did not come home, and the driver, described as "a negro," said on his return that he had left Suber in town. Questioned further, the driver said that Suber would not be coming back because he had gone off with the money for Moore's cotton. According to the report, the family suspected as much and kept the matter quiet for several days.

Suber's neighbors, meanwhile, accused the driver of having murdered and robbed him and were "entertaining serious intentions of lynching the darkey." Before they acted, Suber was discovered alive at Spartanburg, which bore out the driver's second account.
The coverage gives no name for the driver, no number or names for the neighbors, and no follow-up on what happened to Suber or the money.

The only report found ran on August 29, 1888, as an unsigned paragraph in the "South Carolina News" column of the Yorkville Enquirer. The paper told the story as a missing-man case with an unexpected ending, giving Suber the title "Mr." and calling the accused man "the negro" and "the darkey." It offered no comment on the neighbors' plan to lynch a man for a killing that had not happened.

bases: The only report describes neighbors who accused a Black man of murder and robbery and were 'entertaining serious intentions of lynching' him, a threatened lynching with no act of violence reported (A1).

No one was killed: the threat ended when the man the driver was accused of killing was found alive at Spartanburg (A1). The neighbors' intent rested on an accusation of murder and robbery, but no group gathered or acted, according to the report (A1).
One unsigned paragraph in the Yorkville Enquirer is the only report found (A1).
